etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English peril, from Old French peril, from Latin perīculum. Doublet of periculum.

definitions.definition: A situation of serious and immediate danger.
Something that causes, contains, or presents danger.
(insurance) An event which causes a loss, or the risk of a specific such event.
(transitive) To cause to be in danger; to imperil; to risk. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 1830, Robert Hayne, Speech in the United States Senate:
quote.text: And are we, Mr. President, who stood by our country then, who threw open our coffers, who bared our bosoms, who freely perilled all in that conflict, to be reproached with want of attachment to the Union?

quote.citation: 1891, Oscar Wilde, chapter XIV, in The Picture of Dorian Gray, London, New York, N.Y., Melbourne, Vic.: Ward Lock & Co., →OCLC:
quote.text: "I will have nothing to do with this matter, whatever it is. Do you think I am going to peril my reputation for you?"
